name: Prediction Track Records
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Judge the Forecaster, Not Just the Forecast
lesson.summary: A forecaster's credentials matter less than their track record, so judging any technology claim means checking who has been right before, and by how much.
lesson.body:
Once you accept that technology forecasting is structurally hard, and that most hyped technologies underperform their own promises, the next useful move is to stop evaluating each new prediction in isolation and start looking at track records: how has a given forecaster, institution, or genre of prediction actually done historically.

Track records matter more than credentials because expertise in the underlying science does not automatically transfer into forecasting skill. Judging engineering difficulty, market behavior, and the pace of complementary technologies requires a different kind of judgment than research expertise does. Philip Tetlock's long running research on expert political and geopolitical forecasting found that many credentialed experts performed little better than chance on specific, falsifiable predictions, while a smaller group of careful, self correcting forecasters did meaningfully better over time. The analogy to technology forecasting is not exact, but the underlying lesson, that forecasting is a distinct and measurable skill, generalizes reasonably well.

Nuclear fusion timelines are instructive here specifically as a track record rather than just an example of forecasting difficulty. Researchers and institutions across decades independently produced similarly optimistic thirty year estimates that did not visibly converge or improve in accuracy over time. A pattern of consistently missing in the same optimistic direction across a long enough sample is more diagnostic than any single missed forecast would be on its own.

Moore's Law offers a useful counter example of a forecast track record that held up well. Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit would roughly double on a regular cadence proved remarkably accurate as a track record for decades, which is part of why semiconductor industry roadmaps built around it earned unusual credibility over time. Not every domain, and not every forecaster, has a track record this poor or this good, and telling the two apart is the whole point of tracking records rather than trusting any single claim.

A practical method follows from this. When assessing a claim about a technology's timeline, ask who is making it, a lab with something to sell, an independent academic, a journalist summarizing a press release, what their specific track record on similar claims has been, whether the claim is falsifiable and dated rather than permanently a decade away, and whether the forecaster has publicly revised past predictions when they proved wrong. Forecasters and institutions willing to be graded, and who actually update, deserve more weight than those who quietly move the goalposts.

That is the discipline this book tries to apply to quantum computing claims specifically: not trust the optimists or trust the skeptics, but track, where the record actually exists, whose specific quantum computing predictions have held up over the past decade or two, and weight accordingly, while being honest that quantum computing is young enough that many of its track records are still short.
